html: With type 2 diabetes, insulin doesn't move sugar out of the blood as well as it should, so glucose levels climb. Left unmanaged, the extra sugar can damage blood vessels and organs over the years.

• Feeling thirsty and needing to urinate often
  • Unusual tiredness
  • Cuts or sores that are slow to heal
  • Blurry vision
  • Often, no signs at all in the early years
A blood test such as the A1C shows your average blood sugar over the past few months. Your primary care team can tell you when to start testing and how often.

• Build meals around vegetables, whole grains and lean protein
  • Move your body most days
  • Take medicines as prescribed and check your sugar as advised
  • Keep up with eye exams, foot checks and kidney tests
You feel confused, are vomiting, can't keep fluids down, or have a reading far outside the range your care team gave you.

title: Type 2 diabetes
abstract: What happens to blood sugar in type 2 diabetes, how it's found and how people live well with it.
